extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical Euclidean geometry (students, teachers, historians of mathematics)
extracted.subtask_description: Statements, definitions, constructions, and proofs from Euclid's Elements (Books II–III) presenting classical plane-geometry propositions and constructions and their justifying arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. II.IX (Book II) — squares when line divided equally and unequally
rubrics_metrics.description: IF a straight line be divided into two equal, and also into two unequal parts; the squares of the two unequal parts are together double of the square of half the line, and of the square of the line between the points of section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs a right angle at the midpoint, draws parallels through the unequal division point, and uses equality of corresponding squares in right triangles to show the sum of squares on the unequal parts equals twice the square on half the line plus the square on the segment between section points. (Full constructive proof and stepwise equalities are given.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. II.X (Book II) — relation for bisected and produced line
rubrics_metrics.description: IF a straight line be bisected, and produced to any point, the square of the whole line thus produced, and the square of the part of it produced, are together double of the square of half the line bisected, and of the square of the line made up of the half and the part produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction mirrors Prop. IX by erecting a perpendicular equal to the half, drawing parallels and joining points; the proof uses right-angle square relations and equality arguments to deduce the stated identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. II.XI (Book II) — divide line so whole×part = square of other part (problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: TO divide a given straight line into two parts, so that the rectangle contained by the whole and one of the parts shall be equal to the square of the other part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: describe a square on AB, bisect AC, extend and transfer segments to form another square; use equalities of rectangles and squares and subtraction of common parts to obtain point H on AB such that AB·BH = (AH)^2. Full geometric construction and explanation provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. II.XII (Book II) — obtuse triangle squares relation
rubrics_metrics.description: IN obtuse angled triangles, if a perpendicular be drawn from any of the acute angles to the opposite side produced, the square of the side subtending the obtuse angle is greater than the squares of the sides containing the obtuse angle, by twice the rectangle contained by the side upon which, when produced, the perpendicular falls, and the straight line intercepted without the triangle between the perpendicular and the obtuse angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces the claim to algebraic identities of segments by considering BD divided at C and adding square of the perpendicular DA; uses right-triangle square equalities to show the asserted excess equals twice the rectangle BC·CD.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. II.XIII (Book II) — acute triangle squares relation
rubrics_metrics.description: IN every triangle, the square of the side subtending any of the acute angles is less than the squares of the sides containing that angle, by twice the rectangle contained by either of these sides, and the straight line intercepted between the perpendicular let fall upon it from the opposite angle, and the acute angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof treats cases (perpendicular falls within triangle, outside, or is itself perpendicular) and uses decomposition into squares and rectangles via right triangles to show the stated deficit equals twice the rectangle CB·BD (or DB·BC depending on configuration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. II.XIV (Book II) — construct square equal to given rectilineal figure (problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: TO describe a square that shall be equal to a given rectilineal figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: convert the given figure to an equal rectangular parallelogram, adjust sides by extending and bisecting, describe a semicircle on the extended side, and use right-angle/square relationships to convert the rectangle into a square equal to the original rectilineal figure. The proof shows equalities by removing common squares.

rubrics_metrics.name: Def. III.I — equal circles
rubrics_metrics.description: EQUAL circles are those of which the diameters are equal, or from the centres of which the straight lines to the circumferences are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text remarks this is effectively a theorem (if centers coincide the circles coincide) and explains the meaning: equal radii or diameters define equal circles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Def. III.II — tangent (a line that touches a circle)
rubrics_metrics.description: A straight line is said to touch a circle, when it meets the circle, and being produced does not cut it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defines tangency geometrically (meeting but not cutting when extended).

rubrics_metrics.name: Def. III.III — when circles touch one another
rubrics_metrics.description: Circles are said to touch one another, which meet, but do not cut one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines internal/external touching as meeting at a point without intersection of arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Def. III.IV — straight lines equally distant from centre
rubrics_metrics.description: Straight lines are said to be equally distant from the centre of a circle, when the perpendiculars drawn to them from the centre are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives criterion for equal distance measured by perpendiculars from centre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Def. III.V — farther line
rubrics_metrics.description: And the straight line on which the greater perpendicular falls, is said to be farther from the centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines an order relation for distances of lines from centre via perpendicular lengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Def. III.VI — segment of a circle
rubrics_metrics.description: A segment of a circle is the figure contained by a straight line and the circumference it cuts off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard geometric definition of a circular segment bounded by chord and arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Def. III.VII — the angle of a segment
rubrics_metrics.description: The angle of a segment is that which is contained by the straight line and the circumference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the angle associated to a segment formed between chord and arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Def. III.VIII — angle in a segment
rubrics_metrics.description: An angle in a segment is the angle contained by two straight lines drawn from any point in the circumference of the segment, to the extremities of the straight line which is the base of the segment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies how to form an inscribed angle that stands on the chord (base) of the segment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Def. III.IX — angle standing upon circumference
rubrics_metrics.description: And an angle is said to insist or stand upon the circumference intercepted between the straight lines that contain the angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology for an angle 'standing on' a particular arc (the intercepted arc).

rubrics_metrics.name: Def. III.X — sector of a circle
rubrics_metrics.description: The sector of a circle is the figure contained by two straight lines drawn from the centre, and the circumference between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the region bounded by two radii and the included arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Def. III.XI — similar segments
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar segments of a circle are those in which the angles are equal, or which contain equal angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines similarity for circular segments in terms of their contained/inscribed angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. III.I (Problem) — find centre of given circle
rubrics_metrics.description: To find the centre of a given circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: draw any chord AB, bisect it at D, draw DC at right angles to AB and bisect CE; point F (intersection of perpendicular bisectors) is the centre. Proof: uniqueness of centre argued by triangle congruence and right-angle contradiction; corollary: perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through centre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. III.II — chord joining two circumference points lies within circle
rubrics_metrics.description: IF any two points be taken in the circumference of a circle, the straight line which joins them shall fall within the circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: assuming chord lies outside leads to impossible inequalities of radii/segments when comparing angles and sides; hence chord must fall within the circle (not on or without).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. III.III — line through centre bisecting chord is perpendicular and converse
rubrics_metrics.description: IF a straight line drawn through the centre of a circle bisect a straight line in it which does not pass through the centre, it shall cut it at right angles; and, if it cuts it at right angles, it shall bisect it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses congruent triangles formed by equal radii and common segments to deduce equality of adjacent angles (right angles) and then equality of chord halves by triangle-angle-side arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. III.IV — two chords that don't both pass through centre do not bisect each other
rubrics_metrics.description: IF in a circle two straight lines cut one another which do not both pass through the centre, they do not bisect each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: assume mutual bisection, take centre F, derive contradictory equality of unequal right angles; hence they cannot bisect one another unless both pass through centre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. III.V — two intersecting circles cannot share the same centre
rubrics_metrics.description: IF two circles cut one another, they shall not have the same centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: assume common centre E, draw a chord through intersection and compare equal radii to derive EF = EG contradictions (less to greater).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. III.VI — internally touching circles cannot share centre
rubrics_metrics.description: IF two circles touch one another internally, they shall not have the same centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof analogous to Prop. V: assume same centre yields equality of unequal segments (contradiction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. III.VII — ordering of chords from a point on a diameter
rubrics_metrics.description: IF any point be taken in the diameter of a circle, which is not the centre, of all the straight lines which can be drawn from it to the circumference, the greatest is that in which the centre is, and the other part of that diameter is the least; and, of any others, that which is nearer to the line which passes through the centre is always greater than one more remote: and from the same point there can be drawn only two straight lines that are equal to one another, one upon each side of the shortest line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses triangle inequalities and equal radii comparisons to order lengths of segments from the off-centre point to different circumference points; shows uniqueness of two equal chords symmetric about shortest line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. III.VIII — ordering of lines from external point to concave/convex arcs
rubrics_metrics.description: IF any point be taken without a circle, and straight lines be drawn from it to the circumference, whereof one passes through the centre, of those which fall upon the concave circumference the greatest is that which passes through the centre, and nearer to it are greater than remote; of those on the convex circumference the least is that between the point and the diameter, and nearer to it are less than remote; and only two equal lines can be drawn, one on each side of the least.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof parallels Prop. VII but for an external point, using equal radii and triangle comparisons to order lengths and show existence/uniqueness of symmetric equal segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. III.IX — internal point with more than two equal chords is centre
rubrics_metrics.description: IF a point be taken within a circle, from which there fall more than two equal straight lines to the circumference, that point is the centre of the circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: assume another centre E; the diameter through E would give ordering of lengths contradicting equality of more than two equal radii from the point; thus the point must be the centre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. III.X — one circumference cannot cut another in more than two points
rubrics_metrics.description: ONE circumference of a circle cannot cut another in more than two points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: assume three intersections B,G,F; take centre K of one circle; then inside other circle there would be more than two equal radii from K, making K the centre of both circles which contradicts Prop. V. Hence at most two intersection points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. III.XI — centres line produced passes through internal contact point
rubrics_metrics.description: IF two circles touch each other internally, the straight line which joins their centres being produced shall pass through the point of contact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: assume centre-line doesn't pass through contact point A, derive contradiction by comparing remainders after subtracting common centre distance leading to impossible greater/less relations; hence centres' line passes through contact point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. III.XII — centres line passes through external contact point
rubrics_metrics.description: IF two circles touch each other externally, the straight line which joins their centres shall pass through the point of contact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof analogous to Prop. XI: assume centre-line misses contact A, use equality of radii to form contradictory equalities of whole and parts; conclude centres' line must pass through point of contact.
